A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Sparsing Law study. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed and relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, sparsity scaling curves, activation-pattern analyses, and downstream benchmark results, including Appendix H.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds downstream metric comparisons, CETT sensitivity measurements, a 2.4B training experiment, and decoding-speed measurements.

M1.justification: PPL-p% becomes CETT-PPL-p%, with CETT-PPL-1% emphasized, but the layer-wise thresholding and binary-search procedure remain unchanged. MiniCPM is redescribed as a muP Transformer without a demonstrated architecture change. The 2.4B experiment applies the existing approach.

E1.justification: The training corpora and downstream benchmark suite are retained. Appendix L adds a short-prefix C4 decoding scenario for evaluating serving efficiency. This extends the evaluation scenario without introducing a new data domain; the larger model alone does not change coverage.

E2.justification: The original zero-threshold ReLU, Top-k, FAT-epsilon, and MoE comparisons remain. Figure 3 additionally evaluates the metric comparators on the existing downstream task groups, and Appendix L introduces an evaluated PowerInfer-versus-llama.cpp speed comparison. CETT's relabeling does not introduce a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 2.4B configuration trained on approximately 800B tokens, with a batch size of 2.10 million tokens. It also introduces a serving protocol using 100 C4 prompts with five prefix tokens and CUDA-enabled frameworks on the same A800-equipped machine. These substantially extend the experimental settings; the original benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation through downstream performance-versus-sparsity curves comparing recognition methods (Figure 3), CETT sweeps testing the monotonicity underlying binary search (Figure 15), and a larger-scale test of the fitted sparsity law (Figure 11). The earlier loss, layer-wise, dataset-wise, and token-wise analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed replications, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Both retain the same last-five-checkpoint averaging strategy for stabilizing sparsity measurements. The new average decoding speeds do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds downstream trade-off and CETT sensitivity results, a 2.4B fitted activation limit of 6.48% (93.52% sparsity), and speeds of 41.79 versus 10.23 tokens/second. Tables 4–6 are unchanged after renaming. However, Table 1 introduces a −0.2 commonsense-score decrement for 0.8B ReLU at 10% tolerance, inconsistent with the retained 56.8 dense and 55.6 sparse scores, which imply −1.2.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), including the FFN and CETT definitions, scaling-law functional forms, and neuron-grouping derivation, are retained. The new fitted coefficients and empirical monotonicity plot do not add or revise formal mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on sparsity measurement, scaling observations, and architectural guidance. v2 adds practical model construction as an explicit main research question and claims a 2.4B model with 93.52% sparsity and 4.1× speedup in the abstract and introduction. This extends the claimed contribution to demonstrated serving efficiency.

C2.justification: v2 attributes degradation in very deep models to training instability and adds discussion distinguishing input-dependent activation sparsity from static weight pruning. It removes v1's explicit limitation concerning untested models above 7B, although the largest reported model is 2.4B. Appendix L newly acknowledges that llama.cpp cannot correctly execute the ReLU model used in the speed comparison.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the 2.4B parameter count and batch size, plus serving-framework, CUDA, hardware, and prompt details in Appendix L. It removes v1's explicit SparsingLaw repository and code/checkpoint availability statement. This establishes a documentation change, not that the resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against static weight pruning, citing SparseGPT and Sheared LLaMA without evaluating them as baselines. It also expands interpretability and depth-related citations while removing some earlier robustness references. ProSparse's updated publication citation refers to the same work.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around three research questions. Measurement, influential factors, and practical construction receive separate sections; the methodology material is redistributed, and the MoE discussion and limitations move to appendices. Terminology is revised throughout, including the metric name.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and extensively rearranges displays. It adds Figures 3, 11, and 15, relocates the MoE plot to Appendix B, revises diagram labels, and converts Table 1 from absolute sparse scores to differences from dense scores with an average column. Tables 2 and 3 gain 2.4B entries.

improvement.justification: The new downstream comparisons and CETT sensitivity checks strengthen the metric's empirical justification, while the 2.4B experiment extends support for the scaling findings. Clearer organization also helps. These provide a limited net improvement, tempered by the incompatible dense comparator behind the headline speedup, the new Table 1 inconsistency, and removal of the repository-access statement and explicit above-7B limitation.
